blocks.text: The score could not be trusted

Philips used an adoption score to understand how closely products followed its Design Language System. The score helped product groups see gaps and decide where improvement work belonged on their roadmaps.

Producing it, however, depended on spreadsheets stored across shared drives. Different teams interpreted the criteria differently, only one person could audit a product at a time, and changes were difficult to trace. The problem was larger than slow administration: people were making decisions from a score whose production process lacked consistency and accountability.

items: Teams applied the same scoring criteria differently.
It was difficult to see who changed a score, when or why.
Users moved between spreadsheets, shared drives and separate DLS guidance.
Product owners could not see portfolio gaps without assembling their own summaries.

blocks.label: Product challenge
blocks.text: Make adoption measurable without pretending that a subjective process had suddenly become objective.
I followed the score across three roles

I planned and conducted ten interviews: four product owners, four product designers and two business partners. Rather than asking only what they wanted in a new interface, I followed how the score was created, reviewed and used.

rows: Guidance, progress and less repetitive documentation
A portfolio overview and visible score history
Comparable results and clearer improvement areas

blocks.text: It would be great if we could have a dashboard of sorts that gave a summary of everything.
The interviews shifted the project away from simply digitising the spreadsheet. The tool needed to support the decisions made before, during and after scoring.

blocks.alt: Map of the people, systems and handoffs involved in adoption scoring
blocks.caption: I mapped scoring as a service to expose the roles, systems and handoffs hidden by the spreadsheet.

blocks.text: Research became product rules
Each recurring research signal became a product decision. This kept the redesign tied to the way teams actually worked rather than to a generic dashboard pattern.

blocks.text: A key trade-off sat between consistency and flexibility. Too much freedom would reproduce the variation of the spreadsheets. Too rigid a workflow would ignore legitimate differences between products. I standardised the shared scoring path while leaving space for evidence and context.

blocks.alt: Current-state journey for a designer completing an adoption score
blocks.caption: The current-state journey made context switching, manual interpretation and low confidence visible.

blocks.alt: User flow for the redesigned adoption scoring workflow
blocks.caption: The redesigned flow brought guidance, evidence and progress into one place.

blocks.text: One workflow had to support two different jobs

The designer completing a score and the product owner reviewing a portfolio were not looking for the same thing. Designers needed the criteria and supporting evidence close to the decision. Product owners needed to see what had changed and where attention was required.
I designed the detailed scoring experience around the designer's task, then used the resulting data to create the portfolio view. This avoided forcing one overloaded screen to serve both audiences.

blocks.alt: Adoption tool product list, scoring form and portfolio summary
blocks.caption: The resulting tool separated portfolio visibility from the work of completing an individual score.

blocks.text: Testing changed what the tool captured

I tested the prototype with five participants. The direction reduced friction, but the sessions exposed a more important gap: a score without enough context still left reviewers guessing. The workflow needed to capture the reasoning behind a result, not only the result itself.

items: To paint a better picture of the score, it would be great if we included more context.
Finally, I do not need to take snapshots of every component in my product.

blocks.text: The automated component list was the clearest success. All five participants responded positively because it removed repetitive documentation and let them focus on custom components and exceptions.

blocks.alt: Annotated adoption-tool prototype used during usability testing
blocks.caption: Testing identified where the scoring form needed more context and clearer evidence.

blocks.alt: Component list used to review design-system adoption
blocks.caption: The component list replaced a manual process of collecting and attaching screenshots.

blocks.label: UX engineering contribution
blocks.title: Keeping the project testable while the central data work was delayed
items: I created a local data structure that reflected the intended backend shape.
The React interface reused the Design Language System it was measuring.
The team could validate scoring logic and interaction before the dependent database work was ready.
The temporary structure kept the prototype aligned with the intended backend handoff.

blocks.text: A faster score became a more useful score
The new workflow reduced a full product score from roughly two days to 48 minutes. Reporting errors fell by 28%, while adoption increased by 37%.

items: Scoring fell from two days to 48 minutes.
Reporting and scoring errors fell by 28%.
Use of the scoring workflow increased by 37%.

blocks.text: The more important change was what teams could do with the result. Designers had clearer guidance while completing a score, and product owners could see gaps without rebuilding the picture in another spreadsheet.

blocks.label: Reflection
blocks.text: A governance tool earns trust when people can see how its judgement was produced, not simply when it produces the judgement faster.
